title: Two counters: passes and fails
idea: TOOL: keep two counters driven by a condition - one counts the yes group, one the no group.

exercises.prompt: You walk a list of scores and want how many PASS (>= 50) and how many FAIL. What do you keep?
options: Two counters - passes and fails - updated by an if/else
exercises.explanation: Each item is either a pass or a fail, so an if/else bumps the matching counter. Two running counts.
80 and 60 pass (2), 30 fails (1). The if/else sends each score to exactly one counter.

exercises.prompt: With an if/else, each item adds to exactly ONE of the two counters, never both.
exercises.explanation: True. else runs only when if did not, so each item lands in one group. passes + fails equals the item count.
fails = fails + 1 grows the fail counter. Output here: 1 1.

exercises.prompt: If you used two separate 'if' statements instead of if/else, when could that go wrong?
options: If the two conditions could both be true, an item might get counted twice
exercises.explanation: if/else guarantees exactly one branch. Two overlapping ifs could count one item in both groups. For pass/fail, if/else keeps them exclusive.

exercises.prompt: Arrange a loop that counts passes (>=50) and fails in [55, 20].
exercises.explanation: Start both at 0, branch each score, print. Output: 1 1.
All three pass, so passes = 3 and fails stays 0. The else branch never runs.

exercises.prompt: What is a quick sanity check on your two counters after the loop?
options: passes + fails should equal how many items you walked
The total should be bigger than both
exercises.explanation: Every item went to exactly one group, so the two counters must add up to the item count. A mismatch means a bug.

exercises.prompt: Two counters are just two running variables, each updated when its own condition holds.
exercises.explanation: True. It is the same multiple-state idea: more than one running value, each with its own update rule.

options: Split items into groups with if/else and count each group separately
exercises.explanation: Grouped counting with if/else and two counters is an everyday use of multiple state variables.
